newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan jobless rate hits annual record,to stay high.
newsitem.headline: Japan jobless rate hits annual record,to stay high.

text.p: Japan's unemployment rate hit a record high last year amid a slow recovery in the economy, and no significant improvement is likely in the near term, the government said on Friday.
The unemployment rate for 1996 rose to 3.4 percent from 3.2 percent the previous year, government data showed.
Although still far below the double-digit rates of some industrialised countries, it was the highest level since 1953, the earliest year for which comparative figures are available.
"It is difficult to expect a sharp fall in the unemployment rate," a government official told reporters.
He said the rate was gradually falling on a month-on-month basis, but it was doing so at a snail's pace.

The monthly data for December, also released on Friday, showed that the jobless rate remained unchanged from November at 3.3 percent. It has been moving between 3.3 and 3.4 percent after hitting a record high of 3.5 percent in May and June.
Economists said a drastic improvement was unlikely in face of a slow recovery by the economy, the outlook for which is clouded by a planned rise in the consumption tax from April.
The economy has been struggling to recover from the long slump that followed the bursting of the 1980s asset "bubble", with the number of bankruptcies still high.
Job conditions may also be hit by the effects of the tax rise, the government official said.

He said there was a strong rise in the number of people employed in the construction industry in December, but that this was due to a so-called "rush in" rise in construction ahead of the planned tax rise.
"We may see a (downward) reaction to that," the official said, implying that there may be a decrease in jobs in the construction sector following the tax increase.
The government plans to raise the consumption tax to five percent from three precent on April 1.
Another factor likely to inhibit any drastic improvement in jobs data is the high level of people classified as voluntarily leaving their jobs.
A record high of 0.87 million people left their jobs voluntarily in 1996, accounting for 38.7 percent of the total number of those unemployed, the government data showed.
The official said the high number of workers seeking to change jobs to help their careers may be behind the rise.
A record high 8.4 percent of those employed wanted to switch jobs, the 1996 data showed.

Meanwhile, another closely watched employment figure, the jobs-to-applicants ratio, improved in 1996, rising to 0.70 from 0.63 in the previous year. This means there were 70 job offers for every 100 applicants.
